title: Syllogisms

steps.title: Treat statements as facts
steps.content: A syllogism asks what must be true if the given statements are true. Do not use real-world knowledge that is not stated.
steps.example: All roses are flowers. All flowers are plants. Therefore, all roses are plants.
steps.tip: Only conclusions forced by the statements are correct.

steps.title: Follow a chain
steps.prompt: Statements: All cats are mammals. All mammals are animals. Which conclusion follows?
steps.explanation: Every cat is a mammal and every mammal is an animal, so every cat is an animal.
hints: Represent each category as a set.
Follow containment from A to B to C.

steps.title: Understand some and no
steps.content: 'Some A are B' means at least one item belongs to both sets. 'No A are B' means the sets do not overlap. 'Some A are not B' means at least one A lies outside B.
steps.tip: A statement about 'some' does not mean 'all'.

steps.title: Avoid an invalid inference
steps.prompt: Statements: All A are B. Some B are C. Does it necessarily follow that some A are C?
steps.explanation: The B items that are C may be outside the A subset. Overlap between A and C is not guaranteed.
hints: The 'some' elements of B may lie outside A.
Try one valid arrangement where the conclusion is false.

steps.title: Use a quick Venn diagram
steps.content: Draw one circle inside another for 'all'. Separate circles for 'no'. For 'some', show a clear overlap or a marker in the relevant region. Test whether the conclusion is true in every arrangement allowed by the statements.

steps.title: Test a conclusion
steps.content: A methodical check prevents plausible-but-false answers.
steps.prompt: Arrange the steps to test a syllogism conclusion.
options: Accept only if true in every valid arrangement
Draw the sets from the statements
Try to find a counterexample arrangement
Read the statements as given facts
steps.explanation: Facts → diagram → counterexample test → accept only if forced.
hints: A single counterexample kills the conclusion.

steps.title: No means disjoint
steps.prompt: Statements: No pens are pencils. Which conclusion follows?
steps.explanation: If the sets do not overlap, no pencil is a pen.

steps.title: Catch the some-to-all error
steps.content: A student concludes 'All students are athletes' from 'Some students are athletes'.
options: 'Some' only guarantees at least one shared case, not every student

feedback_by_option.2: That is the error being diagnosed.
feedback_by_option.3: The statement already allows shared members.
feedback_by_option.4: The statement is possible; the over-strong conclusion is not.

steps.explanation: 'Some students are athletes' does not force every student to be an athlete.
hints: Ask whether every member must satisfy the conclusion.

steps.title: Forced negative conclusion
steps.prompt: Statements: No A are B. Some C are A. Which conclusion follows?
steps.explanation: The C items that are A cannot be B, so at least some C are not B.
hints: Place the overlapping C-A region outside B.
That region proves some C are not B.

questions.prompt: Statements: All A are B. All B are C. Which conclusion follows?
questions.explanation: A ⊆ B ⊆ C implies A ⊆ C.

questions.prompt: Statements: No pens are pencils. Which conclusion follows?
Statements: Some students are athletes. Which conclusion is certain?
questions.explanation: Shared members are both athletes and students.

questions.prompt: All doctors are graduates. Some graduates are artists. Does some doctor is an artist follow?
questions.explanation: Artist-graduates may be outside the doctor group.

questions.prompt: No A are B. Some C are A. Which conclusion follows?
All cats are mammals. All mammals are animals. Conclusion?
questions.explanation: Subset chain forces all cats are animals.

learning_objectives: Translate universal and existential statements into set relationships.
Use subset chains to derive necessary conclusions.
Distinguish all, some and no statements.
Reject conclusions that are not guaranteed by the premises.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Some B are C means some A are C when all A are B.
common_misconceptions.correction: The B elements that overlap C may be outside the A subset.

common_misconceptions.misconception: All A are B means all B are A.
common_misconceptions.correction: Set inclusion is one-directional unless the reverse is stated.

common_misconceptions.misconception: A real-world true statement must follow from the premises.

worked_examples.title: Subset chain
worked_examples.input: All A are B. All B are C.

worked_examples.title: Invalid some-overlap
worked_examples.input: All A are B. Some B are C.
trace: A is a subset of B.
C may touch B outside A.
worked_examples.output: Some A are C does not necessarily follow
worked_examples.explanation: Need a forced overlap with A, not only with B.

worked_examples.title: Forced not-B
worked_examples.input: No A are B. Some C are A.
trace: Part of C is inside A.
worked_examples.explanation: The C∩A region lies outside B.

company_applications.practice: Draw the sets and test whether the conclusion is forced.
Reject conclusions that require an unstated overlap.
Use a counterexample arrangement to test uncertain conclusions.

srs_cards.question: What does 'All A are B' mean?
srs_cards.answer: Every member of A belongs to B; it does not imply every B is A.

srs_cards.question: How can you disprove a syllogism conclusion?
srs_cards.answer: Give one valid arrangement of the premises in which the conclusion is false.

srs_cards.question: What does 'some' guarantee?
srs_cards.answer: At least one shared case — never automatically all members.

quest.story: Service-company reasoning rounds treat statements as closed facts. Accept only forced conclusions.
quest.mission: Use set relationships and Venn diagrams to test necessary conclusions.
success_criteria: Translate all, some and no statements into sets.
Test conclusions in every valid arrangement.
